stage1/problem/A2/v0:
Problem: MVFA's few-shot mode fine-tunes the adapters on K normal plus K abnormal target images with pixel masks; can this labelled support set be replaced by an unlabelled pool of target scans? We ask whether source-free self-training of the segmentation and detection adapters on pseudo-labels from MVFA's own zero-shot maps — where a pixel is pseudo-labelled only if all four feature levels agree (it lies in the lowest or highest 10% of scores at every level) and all other pixels are ignored — improves image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and PRO on a disjoint test split of the target modality, and how many unlabelled scans N are needed to match few-shot MVFA with K = 4 labelled normal and abnormal images. Each target dataset is split 50/50 (by patient where identifiers exist) into the unlabelled pool and the test set.

Rationale: The corrected limitation G4 shows that MVFA's 'K-shot' setting requires 2K annotated target images including masks, while clinical reality at a new site is usually a large unlabelled archive and no annotation budget. Pseudo-label adaptation exists for CLIP-based localisation (AnoCLIP's test-time adaptation), but not for multi-level medical adapters under modality shift, where wrong pseudo-labels can reinforce errors. Agreement across MVFA's four levels is a confidence signal specific to its design, and the number of unlabelled scans needed to match K labelled pairs is a directly actionable answer. This differs from training with image-level labels on the source (the other problem of this group) because the target here has no labels at all. It is implementable with the existing training loop and mask-based losses restricted to confident pixels, and runs on one GPU.
stage1/problem/B2/v0:
Problem: A zero-shot deployment of MVFA has no target labels, so its decision threshold must be chosen on the source modalities; do split-conformal false-positive guarantees calibrated on normal source images survive the shift to an unseen modality, and can a label-free correction repair them? We calibrate per-image anomaly scores (computed without any test-set normalisation, under max-pixel, top-k-mean and mean aggregation) on held-out normal images of the source modalities at nominal false-positive rates of 1%, 5% and 10%, measure the realised false-positive rate and sensitivity on each held-out BMAD modality, and test weighted split conformal prediction, where calibration images are weighted by a density ratio between source calibration features and the unlabelled target test batch (estimated by a domain classifier on CLIP global features).

Rationale: Limitations G8, G9, G11 and G17 show that MVFA's scores are normalised with test-set statistics, aggregated inconsistently and judged only by AUROC, so its usability at a fixed operating point is unknown — and in the zero-shot setting there is not even a support set to normalise against. Conformal prediction provides guarantees only under exchangeability, which a modality shift violates; how badly, for CLIP-based medical anomaly scores, and whether covariate-shift weighting repairs it, is not addressed by the target paper or by related work, which optimises AUROC through features and prompts. The problem is confined to scoring and thresholding, is inference-only on baseline checkpoints selected under the shared protocol, and its per-modality results tell a practitioner which shifts break the guarantee.
stage1/problem/D2/v0:
Problem: Is MVFA's frozen, template-averaged 'normal' text anchor — one vector shared by brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT, chest X-ray and histopathology — a bottleneck, and can it be made modality-specific without seeing anomalies? As a precondition we measure the variance of MVFA's zero- and few-shot AUROC over 20 random subsets of 5, 10 and 20 of its 35 prompt templates. We then replace the static normal anchor with a support-conditioned one: a light projector, trained on the source modalities, maps the mean adapted feature of the K normal support images to an additive offset of the normal text embedding, while the abnormal side keeps several state-description anchors matched many-to-one. Outcomes: few-shot image- and pixel-level AUROC and PRO per held-out modality, and the template-sensitivity variance.

Rationale: G5 notes that MVFA presumes one universal concept of normality and reports no prompt-sensitivity analysis; G7 notes the symmetric treatment of a compact normal and a diverse abnormal distribution. Related work conditions prompts on the test image (AULoRA, AdaCLIP-style hybrid prompts) or learns object-agnostic prompts (AnomalyCLIP, HieClip); conditioning the normal anchor on the support normals instead gives it a modality-level reference without exposure to anomalies, and the sensitivity analysis decides first whether the text side matters at all. The change is limited to the text-anchor computation of the public code and is cheap on one GPU.
